name: Georgia
summary: A Caucasus country with an ancient Christian kingdom tradition, independent from the USSR in 1991; Abkhazia and South Ossetia are outside its control.

knownFor.label: Georgian alphabet
knownFor.note: Its own script, used since the 5th century.

knownFor.label: Qvevri wine
knownFor.note: Wine made in clay jars, about 8,000 years old.

location.value: The southern Caucasus between the Black Sea and the Caspian region; about 69,700 km² (including Abkhazia and South Ossetia).

terrain.value: The Greater Caucasus mountains in the north, the Lesser Caucasus in the south, and fertile valleys and the Kolkheti lowland between.

climate.value: Mild on the coast, cold in the mountains.

resources.value: Farmland, vineyards, tea and citrus, manganese (Chiatura), and rivers for hydroelectric power.

disasters.value: Earthquakes (Racha, 1991), landslides and floods, such as the 2015 Tbilisi flood.

population.value: About 3.7 million, down from over 5 million in 1989 because of emigration and war.

urbanisation.value: About 60% urban; Tbilisi has over a million people; Batumi and Kutaisi are the next largest cities.

disease.value: Moderate health; tuberculosis and hepatitis C were serious problems, tackled by national programmes.

migration.value: Hundreds of thousands were displaced by the wars in Abkhazia and South Ossetia; many Georgians emigrated for work.

economicBase.value: Farming, wine, tourism, mining and transit trade between the Caspian and the Black Sea.

tradeRoutes.value: The Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan oil pipeline (2006) and the Black Sea ports of Poti and Batumi link the Caspian to Europe.

wealth.value: An upper-middle-income country, still poorer than most of Europe.

moneyAndTax.value: The lari, introduced in 1995 after hyperinflation.

inequality.value: Moderate, with poorer rural areas and many people relying on money sent from abroad.

governmentType.value: A parliamentary republic; a 2017 constitution moved power from the president to parliament and the prime minister.

keyRulers.value: Zviad Gamsakhurdia. Eduard Shevardnadze. Mikheil Saakashvili.

succession.value: Elections to parliament; the largest party forms the government. The 2024 election results were disputed and caused protests.

institutions.value: Parliament, the government, the Constitutional Court and the Georgian Orthodox Church as an influential body.

eliteConflict.value: Strong polarisation between the ruling party and the opposition, especially over relations with Russia and the EU.

armyAndTech.value: Small armed forces trained with NATO help; Georgia sent troops to Iraq and Afghanistan.

majorWars.value: Civil war (1991–93), wars in South Ossetia and Abkhazia (1991–93), and the war with Russia (2008).

territoryChange.value: Abkhazia and South Ossetia are outside government control.

alliancesRivals.value: Seeks EU and NATO membership; EU candidate status (2023); Russia is the main rival.

inventions.value: Few modern inventions; archaeology shows some of the world’s oldest wine-making (about 6000 BCE).

scienceEducation.value: Tbilisi State University (founded 1918) and other universities; high literacy.

openness.value: Open to trade and tourism, with visa-free entry for many countries.

communicationTransport.value: Roads and railways, including the Baku–Tbilisi–Kars railway (2017) linking the Caspian to Turkey.

religion.value: Georgian Orthodox, one of the oldest churches.

languageWriting.value: Georgian, a Kartvelian language with its own alphabet (Mkhedruli); Abkhaz and Ossetian are spoken in the breakaway regions.

artsArchitecture.value: Medieval churches and monasteries (Gelati, Svetitskhoveli), Svan defensive towers, and polyphonic singing (UNESCO).

socialStructure.value: Strong family networks; a gap between Tbilisi and rural areas.

sharedIdentity.value: A strong national identity built on the Georgian language, Orthodox Christianity and a long history of resisting empires.

dailyLife.value: Houses and flats; khachapuri, khinkali, wine.

neighbours.value: Russia to the north, Turkey to the south-west, Armenia and Azerbaijan to the south and east.

ideasReligions.value: Mostly Georgian Orthodox Christian; one of the first Christian kingdoms (about 337).

colonisation.value: Annexed by the Russian Empire (from 1801); briefly independent (1918–21), then part of the Soviet Union until 1991.

riseSignals.value: Declared independence from the Soviet Union in April 1991.

peakPeriod.value: Reforms after the 2003 Rose Revolution cut corruption and sped up growth.

declineSignals.value: Russia recognised Abkhazia and South Ossetia (2008); Georgia and most countries regard them as occupied.
